text: Oliviero Diliberto, born on 13 October 1956 in Cagliari, is an Italian politician who has served as leader of the Party of Italian Communists. He was born into a family of public servants: his father, Marco, worked as an attorney in the Administration of the Region of Sardinia, and his mother, Lella, was a teacher. The death of his father in 1971 deeply affected him, after which he took on a fatherly role for his younger siblings, his sister Ludovica (then eight years old) and his brother Alessio, who was born two months before. At age 13 in 1969, during a period of turmoil in Italian schools, Diliberto became involved in the student movement and rose through the ranks of the student activism. In 1978, the same year he graduated, he became Secretary of the FGCI (Federation of Young Italian Communists, the youth organization of the PCI) for the province of Cagliari. After graduating from high school, he traveled to Paris, where he briefly worked at the city morgue to support himself, preparing corpses for autopsies, a period influenced by his fascination with Michel Foucault's philosophical thought. From 1978 to 1986, he earned scholarships to study law in Frankfurt and Rome, and later worked as a researcher at the University of Cagliari, eventually becoming a Professor of Roman Law. A former member of the Italian Communist Party, he joined the Communist Refoundation Party following the breakup of his former party. First elected as a Member of Parliament in 1994 for the Communist Refoundation Party, he left the party in 1998 in opposition to the leadership's stance on a motion of no confidence that resulted in Romano Prodi's defeat. Alongside Armando Cossutta and others, he founded the Party of Italian Communists, of which he became secretary. He served as Minister of Justice in the first government of Massimo D'Alema, becoming one of only two party members in that government, holding the position until 2000 when he voluntarily stepped down to focus on party affairs. Upon taking office as Minister of Justice, he expressed pride in being "The second Communist appointed as Minister of Justice after Palmiro Togliatti" and had the same desk previously used by Togliatti restored and placed in his office. In November 2004, he faced widespread criticism for meeting with Hizbollah leader Sheik Hassan Nasrallah during a visit to Lebanon, prompting a protest note from the Israeli Ambassador in Rome. Before the April 2006 general election, which was won by the centre-left coalition, he declared he would not serve as minister if the centre-left won, instead remaining as party leader—a position he has maintained. In May 2006, he was elected to the City Council of Rome. He is currently a professor of Roman Law at the Faculty of Law of the "La Sapienza" University of Rome. Before the April 2008 snap general election, caused by the fall of the Prodi II Cabinet, he refused to run for the Camera dei Deputati in the Turin constituency for the left-wing alliance The Left – The Rainbow, on the grounds of giving a chance to a junior party fellow—a steel worker at the local Thyssen-Krupp steelworks, who died in a fire on 6 December 2007 that killed seven colleagues. After the poor results of both the 2008 general election and the 2009 European election, in which the Italian left-wing parties failed to reach the minimum threshold, Diliberto was confirmed as party secretary with a mandate to promote unity among left-wing parties. Diliberto has been married twice: he married Ms. Delia Cardia in 1985, after which they separated, and is currently married (since 1997) to Ms. Gabriella Serrenti, whom he met in 1978 at the university where he was an assistant lecturer.
